summary: Exploring the Moon’s south pole presents several challenges including complex lighting conditions uneven terrain and communication limitations. Some areas experience long periods of sunlight, while others remain permanently or temporarily shadowed. Additionally direct communication with Earth depends on its position relative to the lunar horizon.BADER is an interactive lunar exploration platform designed to help users evaluate potential landing locations and dates at the Moon’s south pole. The platform combines location-based analysis with time dependent astronomical information to provide a clearer understanding of environmental conditions that may affect future lunar missions.Users can select a location on the lunar surface and choose a specific date to explore the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the local horizon. This visualization helps assess sunlight availability for solar power generation and identify potential direct-to-Earth communication opportunities.BADER uses NASA-supported scientific data and tools, including lunar coordinates, terrain information, and NASA SPICE-based astronomical calculations.The platform aims to support researchers, mission planners, educators, students, and lunar exploration enthusiasts. By bringing important environmental information together in one accessible interface, BADER helps users compare locations and dates, understand mission constraints, and make more informed preliminary decisions when planning future lunar missions.
details:
What is BADER?

BADER is an interactive website that helps people explore the Moon and compare locations and dates for a surface mission. It shows when a mission could meet its needs for sunlight and a clear view of Earth.

Why does it matter?

Near the Moon’s south pole, the Sun stays low in the sky. A nearby ridge can block sunlight or hide Earth from view. These conditions change over time, so both the landing site and the mission start date matter.

How does it work?

Users can explore 21 locations on a 3D Moon, see local terrain where available, and compare up to four supported sites. They choose a date range, enter how long the mission will last, and set the longest stretches it can go without sunlight or a view of Earth. BADER uses the local terrain to check when the Sun and Earth are visible and shows which start times meet those limits.

What makes BADER different?

BADER applies the "same mission requirements" to multiple sites and checks sunlight and Earth visibility together. In our example, Connecting Ridge had sunlight throughout the 30-day search period. When we checked both requirements for the same three-day mission, 337 out of 649 start times fit at IM‑2 Athena and 270 out of 649 fit at Connecting Ridge. That comparison helps users decide which sites and dates are worth studying further.

How did we build it?

We built a web app for exploring the Moon and a Python service for the calculations. We used NASA’s SPICE toolkit to calculate the positions of the Sun and Earth, LOLA elevation data to model the terrain, and NASA imagery for the globe. We checked the position calculations against JPL Horizons across 1,050 samples. [NASA SPICE](https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/naif/) · [LOLA data](https://pgda.gsfc.nasa.gov/products/90) · [Moon imagery](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4720/) · [JPL Horizons](https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons/)

The prototype gives students, researchers, and mission teams a way to explore lunar terrain and make early comparisons before more detailed mission studies. [Explore BADER](https://bader.g7logic.com/)
